questions.stem: Which of the following gives the correct order of the stages of mitosis?
questions.explanation: The chromosomes first become visible (prophase), then line up at the equator (metaphase), then their chromatids are pulled apart (anaphase), and finally two new nuclei form (telophase). The initials spell PMAT, which is worth memorising.

distractorRationale.a: Chromosomes cannot line up before they have condensed and become visible
distractorRationale.c: Chromatids cannot be pulled apart before the chromosomes have lined up on the spindle
distractorRationale.d: Interphase precedes mitosis but is not one of its stages

questions.stem: How many daughter cells are produced when one cell completes meiosis?
questions.explanation: Meiosis consists of two successive divisions. The first gives two haploid cells and the second divides each of those, so four haploid cells result altogether.

distractorRationale.b: Two is the number produced by mitosis, or by meiosis I alone
distractorRationale.a: One cell entering division must produce more than one cell
distractorRationale.d: Eight would require a third division, which does not occur in meiosis

questions.stem: A body cell of a certain animal contains 24 chromosomes. How many chromosomes will each of its sperm cells contain?
questions.explanation: Sperm cells are gametes formed by meiosis, which halves the chromosome number. Half of the diploid 24 is the haploid number 12, so fertilisation with a 12-chromosome egg restores 24 in the zygote.

distractorRationale.a: Halving twice; meiosis halves the number once, not once per division
distractorRationale.c: This is the diploid body-cell number, which would apply only if gametes were formed by mitosis
distractorRationale.d: Doubling instead of halving

questions.stem: At which stage of mitosis do the chromosomes line up along the equator of the cell?
questions.explanation: In metaphase each chromosome takes up a position on the equatorial plate with its centromere attached to a spindle fibre. This arrangement is what allows the two chromatids to be pulled in opposite directions in the next stage.

distractorRationale.a: In prophase the chromosomes are condensing and the spindle is only beginning to form
distractorRationale.c: In anaphase the chromatids are already moving away from the equator towards the poles
distractorRationale.d: In telophase the chromosomes have reached the poles and new nuclei are forming

questions.stem: Crossing over during meiosis is important because it

options.text: doubles the chromosome number of the gametes
produces new combinations of genes, increasing variation
ensures that all gametes are genetically identical
repairs damaged cells in the body

questions.explanation: While homologous chromosomes are paired in prophase I, their chromatids may exchange equivalent segments. Each chromosome then carries a mixture of maternal and paternal alleles, so the gametes contain gene combinations that neither parent had.

distractorRationale.a: Crossing over exchanges segments; it does not change chromosome number, which meiosis halves
distractorRationale.c: Crossing over does the opposite — it makes gametes differ from one another
distractorRationale.d: Repair of body tissue is achieved by mitosis, not meiosis

questions.stem: In which of the following would mitosis, rather than meiosis, be taking place?

options.text: The anther of a hibiscus flower
The root tip of a maize seedling
The ovule of a mango tree

questions.explanation: A root tip is a growing region, and growth requires many identical diploid cells, which only mitosis can supply. Anthers, testes and ovules are reproductive structures where meiosis produces gametes or spores.

distractorRationale.a: Pollen grains are formed in the anther by meiosis
distractorRationale.c: Sperm cells are formed in the testis by meiosis
distractorRationale.d: The egg cell is formed in the ovule by meiosis

questions.stem: Interphase is the stage of mitosis during which the chromatids are pulled to opposite poles of the cell.
questions.explanation: False on two counts. Interphase is not a stage of mitosis at all — it is the period before division when the cell grows and duplicates its DNA. Chromatids are pulled to the poles during anaphase.

questions.stem: If gametes were produced by mitosis instead of meiosis, what would happen to the chromosome number of a species over successive generations?

options.text: It would double in every generation
It would be halved in every generation
It would stay the same but variation would increase

questions.explanation: Mitosis keeps the chromosome number the same, so both gametes would be diploid. Fertilisation adds the two sets together, so a 46 + 46 fusion would give 92, then 184, and so on. Meiosis exists precisely to halve the number in advance so that fertilisation restores it.

distractorRationale.a: The number stays constant only because meiosis halves it before fusion
distractorRationale.c: Halving is what meiosis does; mitosis does not reduce chromosome number
distractorRationale.d: Mitosis produces identical cells, so variation would fall rather than rise

questions.stem: A plant cell and an animal cell both complete telophase. Which difference will be seen as the cytoplasm divides?

options.text: The animal cell forms a cell plate while the plant cell pinches inwards
The plant cell forms a cell plate while the animal cell membrane pinches inwards
Only the animal cell divides its cytoplasm
Both cells form a cellulose plate across the equator

questions.explanation: A plant cell is boxed in by a rigid cellulose wall, so it cannot pinch; instead vesicles fuse along the equator to build a cell plate that becomes a new middle lamella and wall. An animal cell has only a flexible membrane, so a ring of protein constricts it like a drawstring.

distractorRationale.a: The two mechanisms have been swapped
distractorRationale.c: Both cell types complete cytokinesis, otherwise no new cells would form
distractorRationale.d: Animal cells have no cellulose, so they cannot build a cellulose plate

questions.stem: State four differences between mitosis and meiosis, and give two reasons why meiosis is described as biologically important.
markingGuide: Any four valid differences, one mark each: number of divisions (one versus two); number of daughter cells (two versus four); chromosome number of daughter cells (unchanged versus halved); genetic make-up (identical versus different); pairing of homologous chromosomes and crossing over absent versus present; site of occurrence (somatic growing tissue versus gonads, anthers and ovules)
Importance 1: meiosis halves the chromosome number so that fertilisation restores the diploid number instead of doubling it in each generation (2 marks)
Importance 2: crossing over and independent assortment create genetic variation, which is the raw material for adaptation, natural selection and selective breeding (2 marks)
questions.explanation: The differences are best given as matched pairs so the comparison is explicit. The two standard reasons for the importance of meiosis are the maintenance of a constant chromosome number across generations and the generation of genetic variation.

questions.stem: During which phase of mitosis do the sister chromatids separate and move toward opposite poles?
questions.explanation: During anaphase, the sister chromatids are pulled apart by the spindle fibers and move toward opposite poles of the cell. This separation is crucial for ensuring that each daughter cell receives an identical set of chromosomes.

distractorRationale.a: Prophase is the stage where chromatin condenses into visible chromosomes, but sister chromatids do not separate at this stage.
distractorRationale.b: In metaphase, chromosomes align at the equatorial plane, but they have not yet separated.
distractorRationale.d: Telophase is the final stage where the cell prepares to divide, but the chromatids have already separated.

questions.stem: What is the primary purpose of meiosis in sexual reproduction?

options.text: To produce gametes with half the chromosome number
To increase the number of chromosomes

questions.explanation: The primary purpose of meiosis is to produce gametes, which are haploid cells containing half the chromosome number of the parent cell. This reduction is essential for maintaining the species' chromosome number during fertilization.

distractorRationale.a: Producing identical cells is a function of mitosis, not meiosis.
distractorRationale.c: Repairing damaged tissues is not a function of meiosis; it is related to mitosis.
distractorRationale.d: Meiosis reduces the chromosome number, rather than increasing it.

questions.stem: Which of the following statements correctly compares mitosis and meiosis?

options.text: Mitosis results in four daughter cells; meiosis results in two.
Mitosis involves two rounds of cell division; meiosis involves one.
Meiosis results in genetically diverse cells; mitosis results in identical cells.
Mitosis occurs only in reproductive cells; meiosis occurs in somatic cells.

questions.explanation: Meiosis results in genetically diverse cells due to processes such as crossing over and independent assortment, while mitosis produces identical daughter cells for growth and repair. This genetic diversity is crucial for evolution and adaptation.

distractorRationale.a: Mitosis results in two daughter cells, while meiosis results in four.
distractorRationale.b: Mitosis involves one round of cell division, while meiosis involves two.
distractorRationale.d: Mitosis occurs in somatic cells, while meiosis occurs in reproductive cells.

questions.stem: What is the term for the period of the cell cycle where the cell prepares for mitosis?
questions.explanation: Interphase is the phase where the cell grows and prepares for mitosis by duplicating its DNA and organelles. This stage is crucial for ensuring that the daughter cells have all the necessary components after division.

distractorRationale.b: Cytokinesis is the process of cytoplasm division after mitosis, not a preparatory phase.
distractorRationale.c: Telophase is the final stage of mitosis where the chromosomes de-condense.
distractorRationale.d: Prophase is the first stage of mitosis, not a preparatory phase.

questions.stem: In which phase of meiosis does crossing over occur?
questions.explanation: Crossing over occurs during Prophase I of meiosis, where homologous chromosomes exchange genetic material. This process increases genetic variation in the resulting gametes, which is vital for evolution.

distractorRationale.a: Metaphase I is where chromosomes align at the equator, but no crossing over occurs.
distractorRationale.b: Anaphase I is the stage where homologous chromosomes are pulled apart.
distractorRationale.d: Telophase I is the stage where the cell prepares to divide, not where crossing over occurs.

questions.stem: What is the chromosome number of the daughter cells produced by meiosis if the parent cell has 16 chromosomes?
questions.explanation: If the parent cell has 16 chromosomes, meiosis will reduce the chromosome number by half in each daughter cell, resulting in 8 chromosomes. This reduction is essential for maintaining chromosome numbers across generations.

distractorRationale.b: Daughter cells produced by meiosis have half the chromosome number of the parent cell.
distractorRationale.c: Meiosis produces four daughter cells, each with half the chromosome number, which would be 8 in this case.
distractorRationale.d: Meiosis does not increase the chromosome number; it reduces it.

questions.stem: Which of the following best describes the outcome of mitosis?
questions.explanation: Mitosis results in the formation of two genetically identical daughter cells, each with the same number of chromosomes as the parent cell. This is essential for growth, repair, and asexual reproduction.

distractorRationale.b: Four genetically diverse cells are produced by meiosis, not mitosis.
distractorRationale.c: Mitosis produces identical cells, not diverse ones.
distractorRationale.d: Mitosis produces two cells, not four.

questions.stem: What is the result of cytokinesis in a plant cell?
questions.explanation: In plant cells, cytokinesis results in the formation of a cell plate that eventually develops into a new cell wall, separating the two daughter cells. This is different from animal cells, which form a cleavage furrow.

distractorRationale.b: Cleavage furrow formation is characteristic of animal cells during cytokinesis.
distractorRationale.c: New organelles are not formed specifically during cytokinesis; they are replicated during interphase.
distractorRationale.d: Sister chromatids are separated during anaphase, not formed during cytokinesis.

questions.stem: Which of the following processes ensures genetic variation in meiosis?
questions.explanation: Independent assortment during meiosis allows for the random distribution of maternal and paternal chromosomes into gametes, contributing to genetic variation. This process, along with crossing over, is vital for evolution.

distractorRationale.a: Replication is the process of copying DNA, not directly related to genetic variation.
distractorRationale.c: Cytokinesis is the division of the cytoplasm and does not affect genetic variation.
distractorRationale.d: Mitosis does not introduce genetic variation; it produces identical cells.

questions.stem: What is the primary difference between mitosis and meiosis in terms of chromosome number?

options.text: Mitosis reduces chromosome number; meiosis maintains it.
Mitosis maintains chromosome number; meiosis reduces it.

questions.explanation: Mitosis maintains the chromosome number of the parent cell in the daughter cells, while meiosis reduces the chromosome number by half, resulting in haploid gametes. This distinction is essential for sexual reproduction.

distractorRationale.a: Mitosis does not reduce chromosome number; it maintains it.
distractorRationale.c: Only meiosis reduces chromosome number; mitosis maintains it.
distractorRationale.d: Mitosis maintains chromosome number, while meiosis reduces it.

questions.stem: What is the total number of chromosomes in the daughter cells produced by mitosis if the parent cell has 20 chromosomes?
questions.explanation: Mitosis results in two daughter cells that are genetically identical to the parent cell. Therefore, if the parent cell has 20 chromosomes, each daughter cell will also have 20 chromosomes.

distractorRationale.a: This option represents half the chromosome number, which is incorrect for mitosis.
distractorRationale.c: This option suggests an increase in chromosome number, which does not occur in mitosis.
distractorRationale.d: This option suggests a doubling of chromosome number, which is incorrect for mitosis.

options.text: It produces identical cells for growth.
It ensures the chromosome number is halved for gamete formation.

questions.explanation: Meiosis is crucial for sexual reproduction as it reduces the chromosome number by half, ensuring that when gametes fuse during fertilization, the resulting zygote has the correct diploid number of chromosomes.

distractorRationale.a: This option describes mitosis, not meiosis.
distractorRationale.c: This option refers to a function unrelated to meiosis.

questions.stem: During which phase of mitosis does the nuclear envelope break down?
questions.explanation: During prophase, the chromatin condenses into visible chromosomes, and the nuclear envelope breaks down, allowing the spindle fibers to attach to the chromosomes.

distractorRationale.b: In metaphase, the chromosomes are aligned at the equatorial plane, but the nuclear envelope has already broken down.
distractorRationale.c: Anaphase is the phase where sister chromatids are pulled apart, and the nuclear envelope is not involved.
distractorRationale.d: Telophase is characterized by the reformation of the nuclear envelope, not its breakdown.

distractorRationale.c: This option incorrectly states the outcome of meiosis, which produces haploid cells.
distractorRationale.d: This option describes the result of mitosis, where two diploid cells are produced.
